title: Class 11 supplementary topic library
coverageNote: Original supplementary core-topic lessons, not an exhaustive textbook course or a certified mapping of the complete 2026–27 syllabus. No copied NCERT chapters or authenticated past-paper questions.

modules.title: Sets and representations
modules.goal: Represent collections and reason with unions and intersections.

concepts.explanation: A collection whose membership is unambiguously defined.
A ∩ B contains exactly the elements common to A and B.
A ∪ B contains elements belonging to at least one of A or B.

example.problem: For A={1,2,3} and B={3,4}, find A∪B and A∩B.
steps: List all distinct elements from both sets for the union.
Keep only the element appearing in both sets for the intersection.

activity.prompt: Draw two overlapping circles for students who play chess and students who play football. Include a region for neither.
activity.check: The overlap means both activities; the outer rectangle represents all students being considered.

questions.prompt: Which symbol means an element belongs to a set?
questions.explanation: x∈A states that x is an element of A.
questions.hint: Separate membership from the relation between two sets.

questions.prompt: If A={a,b} and B={b,c}, what is A∩B?
questions.explanation: Only b belongs to both sets.
questions.hint: Look for common elements.

questions.prompt: In a group, 18 like tea, 12 like coffee and 5 like both. How many like at least one?
questions.explanation: 18+12−5=25; otherwise the overlap is counted twice.
questions.hint: Use n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B).

writing.prompt: Explain why the intersection is subtracted in the union-count formula.
points: Adding the two set sizes counts the overlap twice.
Subtracting the overlap once leaves each member counted once.

revision: A∪B: at least one set.
A∩B: both sets.
The empty set has no elements.

modules.title: Angles and trigonometric identities
modules.goal: Connect radians with angles and use a fundamental identity.

concepts.explanation: The angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal in length to the radius.
For angle θ, the unit-circle point is (cos θ, sin θ).
sin²θ+cos²θ=1 follows from the unit circle equation.

example.problem: Find the positive value of cos θ if sin θ=3/5 and θ is acute.
steps: Use cos²θ=1−sin²θ.
Calculate 1−9/25=16/25.
Choose the positive root because θ is acute.
example.answer: cos θ=4/5.

activity.prompt: Mark 0, π/2, π and 3π/2 on a circle; write the sign of sine and cosine in each quadrant.
activity.check: The y-coordinate gives sine and the x-coordinate gives cosine.

questions.prompt: 180° equals how many radians?
questions.explanation: A half turn is π radians.
questions.hint: A complete turn is 2π radians.

questions.prompt: What is sin²θ+cos²θ?
questions.explanation: The squared coordinates of a unit-circle point sum to 1.
questions.hint: Use x²+y²=1.

questions.prompt: If θ lies in quadrant II and sin θ=3/5, what is cos θ?
questions.explanation: Its magnitude is 4/5 and cosine is negative in quadrant II.
questions.hint: First find the magnitude, then determine the sign.

writing.prompt: Derive sin²θ+cos²θ=1 using a unit circle.
points: State x²+y²=1 for a circle of radius 1.
Substitute x=cos θ and y=sin θ.

revision: Radians measure arc length divided by radius.
Check quadrants before selecting square roots.
π radians=180°.

modules.title: Motion in a straight line
modules.goal: Distinguish displacement, velocity and acceleration.

concepts.explanation: The change in position, including direction.
Total displacement divided by elapsed time.
Acceleration remains constant; v=u+at applies over that interval.

example.problem: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final speed and displacement.
example.answer: Final speed 8 m/s; displacement 16 m.

activity.prompt: Sketch a velocity-time graph for an object accelerating uniformly from rest.
activity.check: It is a straight line through the origin; its slope is acceleration and the area below it is displacement.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time.
questions.hint: Divide m/s by seconds.

questions.prompt: A runner returns to the starting point after one lap. Their displacement is:
options: Equal to distance in every case
questions.explanation: Initial and final positions coincide.
questions.hint: Displacement depends on endpoints.

questions.prompt: A velocity changes from −2 m/s to +4 m/s in 3 s. Average acceleration is:
questions.hint: Retain the signs of velocities.

writing.prompt: Explain how an object can travel a nonzero distance yet have zero average velocity.
points: It can return to its initial position.
Total displacement is then zero although total path length is positive.

revision: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector.
Slope of position-time graph gives velocity.
Constant-acceleration equations require constant acceleration.

modules.title: Forces and Newton’s laws
modules.goal: Connect net force to acceleration using a free-body model.

concepts.explanation: The vector sum of all external forces on the object.
For constant mass, net force equals mass times acceleration.
Interaction forces are equal and opposite but act on different objects.

example.problem: A 3 kg trolley has a 10 N forward force and a 4 N opposing force. Find its acceleration.
steps: Choose forward as positive.
Net force is 10−4=6 N.
a=Fnet/m=6/3=2 m/s².
example.answer: 2 m/s² forward.

activity.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram for a book resting on a horizontal table.
activity.check: Weight acts downward and the normal force upward; they balance but are not a Newton third-law pair.

questions.prompt: Which relation gives acceleration for constant mass?
questions.explanation: Newton’s second law rearranges to a=Fnet/m.
questions.hint: Use the net force, not just one force.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object experiences a net force of 8 N. Its acceleration is:
questions.hint: Divide force by mass.

questions.prompt: Why do third-law forces not cancel in a one-object free-body diagram?
options: One is not a real force
questions.explanation: A diagram of one object includes only forces acting on that object.
questions.hint: Identify the object receiving each force.

writing.prompt: Distinguish balanced forces from a Newton third-law pair.
points: Balanced forces act on the same object and sum to zero.
Third-law forces act on two different interacting objects.

revision: Draw the object before drawing forces.
Mass and weight are different quantities.
Zero net force implies constant velocity, including rest.

modules.title: Mole concept and stoichiometry
modules.goal: Convert between mass, moles and particle counts.

concepts.explanation: An amount of substance containing exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified entities.
Mass per mole, commonly expressed in g/mol.
Coefficients in a balanced equation relate amounts in moles.

example.problem: How many moles are present in 18 g of water? Use H=1 and O=16.
steps: Molar mass H₂O=2×1+16=18 g/mol.
Amount n=mass/molar mass=18/18.
example.answer: 1 mol of H₂O.

activity.prompt: Balance 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O and model the ratio using pairs of paper circles.
activity.check: Two hydrogen molecules react with one oxygen molecule to form two water molecules; atoms are conserved.

questions.prompt: Amount in moles is calculated by:
questions.explanation: n=m/M; units g divided by g/mol give mol.
questions.hint: Check the units.

questions.prompt: For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, 3 mol O₂ needs how much H₂?
questions.explanation: The hydrogen-to-oxygen mole ratio is 2:1.
questions.hint: Use balanced coefficients.

questions.prompt: With 1 mol N₂ and 2 mol H₂ in N₂+3H₂→2NH₃, which is limiting?
questions.explanation: One mole N₂ requires 3 mol H₂, but only 2 mol is available.
questions.hint: Compare available amounts to the required ratio.

writing.prompt: Describe a reliable method for identifying a limiting reagent.
points: Balance the equation.
Convert each available amount to moles.
Compare moles divided by the respective coefficient; the smallest value limits progress.

revision: Specify the particle type when counting entities.
Balance first, calculate second.
Mole ratios are not generally mass ratios.

modules.title: Chemical bonding and molecular shape
modules.goal: Connect electron sharing, ion formation and basic molecular geometry.

concepts.explanation: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a structure.
Atoms share electron density, commonly represented by shared electron pairs.
Electron domains around a central atom arrange to reduce repulsion; lone pairs affect shape.

example.problem: Explain why a water molecule is bent rather than linear.
steps: Oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs in the usual Lewis description.
Four electron domains have a roughly tetrahedral arrangement.
Only atom positions define molecular shape, giving a bent molecule.
example.answer: H₂O is bent, with a bond angle about 104.5°.

activity.prompt: Build paper models of CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O; distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular shape.
activity.check: CO₂ is linear, CH₄ tetrahedral and H₂O bent in these simple models.

questions.prompt: A typical covalent bond involves:
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding is associated with shared electron density between atoms.
questions.hint: Think about the role of valence electrons.

questions.prompt: The molecular shape of CH₄ is:
questions.explanation: Four bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon give a tetrahedral shape.
questions.hint: Count domains around carbon.

questions.prompt: Why is CO₂ linear in the basic VSEPR model?
options: Each double bond counts as two separate domains
questions.explanation: Each double bond counts as one domain; two domains arrange opposite each other.
questions.hint: A multiple bond is one electron domain.

writing.prompt: Explain why electron-domain geometry and molecular shape may differ.
points: Electron-domain geometry includes lone pairs and bonds.
Molecular shape describes the arrangement of atomic nuclei.
Water provides a tetrahedral-domain but bent-shape example.

revision: Count electron domains rather than bond lines.
Lone pairs affect bond angles.
Simple bonding models have limits.

modules.title: Cell structures and organisation
modules.goal: Relate organelles to their functions without treating cells as identical.

concepts.explanation: A selectively permeable boundary regulating exchange with the surroundings.
In a typical eukaryotic cell, a membrane-bound compartment containing most DNA.
A site of protein synthesis present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

example.problem: A cell has a membrane-bound nucleus, chloroplasts and a cell wall. Classify it and explain your evidence.
steps: A membrane-bound nucleus identifies eukaryotic organisation.
Chloroplasts support photosynthesis.
This combination is characteristic of a photosynthetic plant cell.
example.answer: A photosynthetic plant eukaryotic cell.

activity.prompt: Sketch a bacterial cell and a typical leaf cell; label structures shared by both.
activity.check: Both have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material and ribosomes; a bacterium lacks a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which structure makes proteins?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA to build polypeptides.
questions.hint: Choose the site of translation.

questions.prompt: A membrane-bound nucleus is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Eukaryotes include plants, animals, fungi and protists.
questions.hint: The feature is not limited to animals.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid comparison?
options: Bacteria and plant cells both have ribosomes
Only bacteria possess a plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are shared; chloroplasts occur only in suitable photosynthetic eukaryotic cells.
questions.hint: Avoid statements beginning with all unless justified.

writing.prompt: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cellular organisation.
points: Both have genetic material, cytoplasm, a membrane and ribosomes.
A typical eukaryotic cell has a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus.

revision: Organelles are linked to functions.
Not every plant cell photosynthesises.
Viruses are not cellular organisms.

modules.title: Photosynthesis and energy conversion
modules.goal: Connect light capture with carbon fixation.

concepts.explanation: Reactions in thylakoid membranes that use light energy to produce ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from water.
In the Calvin cycle, CO₂ is incorporated into organic molecules using ATP and NADPH.
A pigment involved in absorbing light energy in photosynthetic systems.

example.problem: Why does providing light alone not guarantee unlimited photosynthesis?
steps: Photosynthesis also needs CO₂, water, functioning enzymes and appropriate conditions.
If another factor becomes limiting, extra light may not raise the rate.
example.answer: The rate is limited by the least adequate relevant factor under the conditions.

activity.prompt: Draw an input-output diagram for a chloroplast, separating thylakoids from the stroma.
activity.check: Place light reactions at thylakoids; show ATP and NADPH supporting Calvin-cycle reactions in the stroma.

questions.prompt: The oxygen released in oxygenic photosynthesis comes mainly from:
questions.explanation: Water splitting supplies the oxygen released.
questions.hint: Identify the molecule split by the light reactions.

questions.prompt: The Calvin cycle occurs in the chloroplast:
questions.explanation: Carbon-fixation enzymes operate in the stroma.
questions.hint: Separate carbon fixation from thylakoid light reactions.

questions.prompt: CO₂ is scarce but light is abundant. Increasing light alone will usually:
options: Stop water splitting in every case
Have limited benefit because CO₂ limits the rate
questions.explanation: A limiting factor constrains how much extra light can be used productively.
questions.hint: Consider the resource already in shortest supply.

writing.prompt: Explain the connection between light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle.
points: Light reactions produce ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle uses these to support carbon reduction and regeneration reactions.
The two sets of reactions are metabolically linked.

revision: Released oxygen originates from water.
Carbon fixation occurs in the stroma.
The term light-independent does not mean the Calvin cycle only occurs at night.

modules.title: Reading evidence and inference
modules.goal: Separate stated information, inference and unsupported claims.

concepts.explanation: Information directly stated in a passage.
A conclusion supported by textual clues and reasoning.
Specific words or details used to justify an interpretation.

example.problem: Read: “Mira checked the clock again and moved closer to the station entrance.” What can reasonably be inferred?
steps: Repeated clock-checking suggests attention to time.
The station setting suggests an expected arrival or departure.
Do not invent the reason or name of a person she may be meeting.
example.answer: Mira may be waiting anxiously or watching for someone; the text does not establish the exact reason.

activity.prompt: Write one observation, one supported inference and one unsupported claim about the example.
activity.check: Observation: she checks the clock. Inference: she is concerned about time. Unsupported: her brother’s train is exactly 20 minutes late.

questions.prompt: Which is an inference from “dark clouds gathered and people opened umbrellas”?
questions.explanation: Clouds and umbrellas together support a rain-related interpretation.
questions.hint: Choose what the clues support without adding unrelated facts.

questions.prompt: What best supports a reading interpretation?
options: A relevant quoted or paraphrased detail
The length of the answer alone
A guess about the author’s private life
questions.explanation: An interpretation should be grounded in the passage.
questions.hint: Ask which detail demonstrates the claim.

questions.prompt: A passage gives two possible explanations for a character’s silence. Which response is strongest?
options: Choose one with absolute certainty without evidence
Say all interpretations are equally supported
State the uncertainty and weigh evidence for both
questions.explanation: Good reading acknowledges ambiguity while evaluating support.
questions.hint: Avoid pretending that ambiguous evidence proves one answer.

writing.prompt: Explain an inference from a short passage of your choice.
points: State the inference.
Identify a relevant textual detail.
Explain how the detail supports the inference without overstating certainty.

revision: Observation is not inference.
Use evidence for interpretations.
A plausible story is not automatically a supported interpretation.

modules.title: Building a coherent analytical paragraph
modules.goal: Develop a focused claim with evidence and explanation.

concepts.explanation: A sentence establishing the paragraph’s main point.
The logical connection among ideas.
Explanation of how evidence supports a claim, rather than merely repeating it.

example.problem: Improve: “The character is brave. She goes back. It is nice.”
steps: State the claim precisely: the character acts bravely despite danger.
Add the relevant action: she returns to help another person.
Explain that accepting personal risk supports the judgement of bravery.
example.answer: The character shows courage by returning to help someone despite the danger; her choice puts another person’s safety before her own.

activity.prompt: Write a four-sentence paragraph about a character’s decision, then underline the claim and evidence in different colours.
activity.check: The evidence must relate directly to the claim; the explanation should say why it matters.

questions.prompt: A topic sentence mainly:
options: Repeats the title without a claim
questions.explanation: It directs the reader to the idea developed in the paragraph.
questions.hint: Think about the organising purpose.

questions.prompt: Which connector signals contrast?
questions.explanation: However introduces a contrast or qualification.
questions.hint: Select the connector showing a difference.

questions.prompt: Which revision adds analysis?
options: Explain why the character’s action supports the claim
questions.explanation: Analysis links evidence to an interpretation.
questions.hint: Go beyond what happened to why it supports the point.

writing.prompt: Write an analytical paragraph about a decision in a story you have read.
points: Include a focused claim.
Use a relevant event or short quotation.
Explain the connection.
End with a sentence that advances or closes the point.

revision: One paragraph needs one central focus.
Evidence needs explanation.
Connectors should reflect actual logical relationships.

modules.title: भाषा, संदर्भ और अर्थ
modules.goal: वाक्य के संदर्भ से शब्द का उचित अर्थ समझना।

concepts.explanation: वह स्थिति या आसपास का कथन जिससे किसी शब्द या वाक्य का अर्थ स्पष्ट होता है।
शब्द का सीधा और सामान्य अर्थ।
कथन में निहित मुख्य भाव, जिसे पूरे प्रसंग के आधार पर समझा जाता है।

example.problem: “मुश्किल समय में उसके मित्र दीवार बनकर खड़े रहे।” यहाँ “दीवार” का क्या अर्थ है?
steps: वाक्य में मित्रों की सहायता का प्रसंग है।
मित्र सचमुच ईंट की दीवार नहीं बने।
यहाँ शब्द सुरक्षा और सहारे का भाव देता है।
example.answer: मित्रों ने कठिन समय में दृढ़ सहारा दिया।

activity.prompt: “उसकी बात ने नई राह दिखाई” का शाब्दिक अर्थ और संदर्भगत अर्थ अलग-अलग लिखिए।
activity.check: यहाँ “राह” का अर्थ केवल सड़क नहीं, समाधान या दिशा भी हो सकता है।

questions.prompt: भावार्थ लिखते समय सबसे आवश्यक क्या है?
options: मुख्य भाव को अपने शब्दों में स्पष्ट करना
हर शब्द का अलग शब्दार्थ लिखना
questions.explanation: भावार्थ में पूरे कथन का आशय स्पष्ट किया जाता है।
questions.hint: अलग शब्दों के बजाय पूरे प्रसंग पर ध्यान दें।

questions.prompt: “उसकी आँखों में सपने हैं” में “सपने” का संभावित भाव है:
questions.explanation: संदर्भ के अनुसार सपने भविष्य की इच्छाओं का संकेत हो सकते हैं।
questions.hint: वाक्य को सामान्य बोलचाल के अर्थ में समझें।

questions.prompt: एक ही शब्द के दो अर्थों में सही चुनाव कैसे करेंगे?
questions.explanation: संदर्भ बहुअर्थी शब्द के उचित अर्थ का निर्धारण करता है।
questions.hint: आसपास के कथन का उपयोग करें।

writing.prompt: किसी रूपकात्मक वाक्य का भावार्थ लिखिए।
points: वाक्य का प्रसंग बताइए।
शाब्दिक और निहित अर्थ में अंतर स्पष्ट कीजिए।
मुख्य भाव सरल भाषा में लिखिए।

revision: संदर्भ से अर्थ स्पष्ट होता है।
भावार्थ शब्दार्थों की सूची नहीं है।
अपने शब्दों में मूल भाव बनाए रखें।

modules.title: अनुच्छेद में विचारों का क्रम
modules.goal: एक मुख्य विचार पर संगठित अनुच्छेद लिखना।

concepts.explanation: वह केंद्रीय बात जिसके चारों ओर अनुच्छेद विकसित होता है।
वाक्यों और विचारों के बीच तार्किक संबंध।
मुख्य बात को स्पष्ट करने वाला उपयुक्त प्रसंग या तथ्य।

example.problem: “पुस्तकालय का महत्त्व” पर अनुच्छेद की रूपरेखा बनाइए।
steps: आरंभ में पुस्तकालय की भूमिका बताइए।
पढ़ने, खोजने और शांत अध्ययन के लाभ जोड़िए।
एक प्रासंगिक उदाहरण दीजिए।
अंत में मुख्य विचार को आगे बढ़ाते हुए निष्कर्ष लिखिए।
example.answer: भूमिका → संबंधित लाभ → उदाहरण → सार्थक समापन।

activity.prompt: चार वाक्य लिखकर देखें कि प्रत्येक वाक्य मुख्य विषय से जुड़ा है या नहीं।
activity.check: जो वाक्य विषय से नहीं जुड़ता उसे हटाएँ या उचित संबंध स्पष्ट करें।

questions.prompt: एक अच्छे अनुच्छेद का केंद्र क्या होता है?
questions.explanation: एक मुख्य विचार अनुच्छेद को दिशा देता है।
questions.hint: केंद्रित लेखन पर ध्यान दें।

questions.prompt: कारण बताने के लिए कौन-सा शब्द उपयुक्त है?
questions.explanation: क्योंकि कारण प्रस्तुत करता है।
questions.hint: कारण और विरोध में अंतर करें।

questions.prompt: अनुच्छेद में उदाहरण कब उपयोगी है?
options: जब वह मुख्य विचार की जगह ले ले
जब वह मुख्य बात को स्पष्ट करे
जब वह विषय से असंबंधित हो
जब वह प्रमाण के बिना आँकड़े गढ़े
questions.explanation: संबंधित उदाहरण बात को ठोस बनाता है।
questions.hint: उदाहरण का उद्देश्य स्पष्टता है।

writing.prompt: “नियमित अभ्यास का महत्त्व” पर एक अनुच्छेद लिखिए।
points: स्पष्ट मुख्य विचार रखें।
विचारों को तार्किक क्रम में जोड़ें।
उपयुक्त उदाहरण दें।
अनावश्यक दोहराव हटाएँ।

revision: हर वाक्य विषय से जुड़ा हो।
सरल और सटीक भाषा प्रभावी होती है।
संयोजक शब्द संबंध के अनुसार चुनें।

modules.title: Accounting equation and transactions
modules.goal: Analyse business transactions using assets, liabilities and capital.

concepts.explanation: An economic resource controlled by the business from past events with the potential to produce economic benefits.
A present obligation of the business arising from past events.
Assets=Liabilities+Owner’s equity; transactions preserve this equality.

example.problem: An owner invests ₹50,000 cash and the business buys equipment for ₹20,000 cash. Show the equation.
steps: After investment: cash ₹50,000=capital ₹50,000.
After purchase: cash ₹30,000 plus equipment ₹20,000=capital ₹50,000.
example.answer: Assets remain ₹50,000, with no liability and capital ₹50,000.

activity.prompt: Model a ₹10,000 bank loan after the example and update the equation.
activity.check: Cash rises to ₹40,000; total assets ₹60,000=loan ₹10,000+capital ₹50,000.

questions.prompt: Which equation is correct?
questions.explanation: Owner’s equity is the residual after liabilities are deducted from assets.
questions.hint: Rearrange capital=assets−liabilities.

questions.prompt: Buying equipment for cash immediately:
options: Always reduces total assets by the full price
questions.explanation: Cash decreases and equipment increases by the same amount in this simple transaction.
questions.hint: Track both sides of the exchange.

questions.prompt: A business receives a ₹5,000 loan. Which change is correct?
options: Capital rises ₹5,000 and cash is unchanged
questions.explanation: Cash is an asset and the loan is an obligation.
questions.hint: Receiving funds creates both cash and a repayment obligation.

writing.prompt: Explain why an owner’s investment is not business sales revenue.
points: The business entity is treated separately from its owner.
Investment increases owner’s equity.
Revenue arises from earning activities rather than capital contribution.

revision: Every transaction has a dual effect.
Business and owner are separate accounting entities.
A loan receipt is not income.

modules.title: Journal entries and debit-credit reasoning
modules.goal: Record simple transactions through double entry.

concepts.explanation: Each transaction affects at least two accounts with equal total debits and credits.
An increase in an asset is debited and a decrease is credited.
Expenses are normally debited; revenue is normally credited.

example.problem: Record rent paid in cash, ₹2,000.
steps: Rent expense increases: debit Rent Account ₹2,000.
Cash decreases: credit Cash Account ₹2,000.
Confirm equal debit and credit totals.
example.answer: Rent A/c Dr ₹2,000; To Cash A/c ₹2,000.

activity.prompt: Journalise an owner bringing ₹10,000 cash into the business.
activity.check: Debit Cash ₹10,000 and credit Capital ₹10,000.

questions.prompt: An increase in cash is normally:
questions.explanation: Cash is an asset account and increases by debit.
questions.hint: Identify the account type first.

questions.prompt: Cash sales of ₹3,000 require:
questions.explanation: Cash rises and sales revenue rises.
questions.hint: Match the asset and revenue rules.

questions.prompt: Equal debit and credit totals prove that:
options: The entry is arithmetically balanced, but may still contain errors
questions.explanation: An entry in wrong accounts can still balance.
questions.hint: Distinguish balance from full correctness.

writing.prompt: Show how to analyse a transaction before writing its journal entry.
points: Identify the affected accounts.
Classify each account.
Decide which balances increase or decrease.
Apply debit-credit rules and check equality.

revision: Debit does not always mean loss.
Credit does not always mean gain.
Narrations explain transactions.

modules.title: Business objectives and risk
modules.goal: Distinguish objectives, uncertainty and risk.

concepts.explanation: An intended outcome guiding decisions, such as survival, service quality or profit.
Possibility that outcomes differ adversely from expectations.
A person or group affecting, or affected by, the business.

example.problem: A bakery considers a new product. Explain one objective and two risks.
steps: An objective may be meeting customer demand while earning sustainable revenue.
Demand may be lower than expected.
Ingredient costs or supply interruptions may reduce the margin.
example.answer: Objectives define intended outcomes; risk describes uncertain adverse outcomes.

activity.prompt: Create a table of a small business decision, its objective, risk and a possible mitigation.
activity.check: A mitigation can reduce risk without guaranteeing success; a small trial may test demand.

questions.prompt: Which is a stakeholder?
questions.explanation: Employees are affected by and contribute to business activity.
questions.hint: Look for a person or group with a stake.

questions.prompt: A trial launch mainly helps a business:
questions.explanation: A small pilot provides information at limited scale.
questions.hint: Risk reduction differs from a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why can businesses have objectives beyond immediate profit?
options: Long-term survival also depends on customers, staff and responsible operations
questions.explanation: Multiple objectives can support sustained operation.
questions.hint: Consider long-term relationships and obligations.

writing.prompt: Explain how a business can balance profit with service quality.
points: Profit supports continued operation.
Quality helps retain customers and trust.
Short-term cost cuts can undermine long-term outcomes if service deteriorates.

revision: Risk cannot always be eliminated.
Objectives may conflict.
Stakeholders have different interests.

modules.title: Forms of business ownership
modules.goal: Compare sole proprietorship and partnership conceptually.

concepts.explanation: A business owned by one individual, with no separate legal identity in the usual school-level model.
A business relationship in which persons agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any acting for all.
The owner may be personally responsible for business obligations, subject to the relevant legal structure and rules.

example.problem: A small business owner wants more managerial expertise but is concerned about shared control. Compare options.
steps: Remaining a sole proprietor preserves direct control.
Bringing in a partner may add expertise and resources.
Partnership also requires agreement about decisions, profits and responsibilities.
example.answer: The choice involves trade-offs between resources, control and liability.

activity.prompt: Compare ownership, control, continuity and liability for two forms in a table.
activity.check: Avoid treating every partnership as a company; legal structure changes the analysis.

questions.prompt: A sole proprietorship has:
questions.explanation: Sole means one owner.
questions.hint: Distinguish number of owners from number of workers.

questions.prompt: A possible advantage of partnership is:
options: Automatic limited liability in every form
questions.explanation: Partners may contribute complementary knowledge and resources.
questions.hint: Use a possible benefit rather than a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which question should guide choice of ownership form?
options: What control, funding, continuity and liability does the business need?
questions.explanation: Ownership structure should fit business needs and legal consequences.
questions.hint: Compare practical needs and responsibilities.

writing.prompt: Compare a sole proprietorship with an ordinary partnership.
points: Discuss ownership and control.
Compare available resources.
Address liability and continuity carefully.
Mention the importance of agreement and applicable law.

revision: One owner can employ many workers.
Shared skills can bring shared decision-making challenges.
Different legal structures carry different consequences.

modules.title: Scarcity and opportunity cost
modules.goal: Identify trade-offs and the next-best alternative forgone.

concepts.explanation: Resources are limited relative to competing wants.
The value of the next-best alternative forgone when making a choice.
Choosing more of one use may require less of another.

example.problem: You have one free hour and choose revision over the best alternative, a music lesson. Identify opportunity cost.
steps: List feasible alternatives for the same hour.
Choose the best alternative not taken.
Do not add every rejected activity together.
example.answer: The value of the music lesson forgone is the opportunity cost.

activity.prompt: Allocate a fixed weekly study budget among three subjects and explain one trade-off.
activity.check: Opportunity cost depends on the next-best alternative, not just monetary spending.

questions.prompt: Opportunity cost is:
options: Only the price written on a label
Always zero when no money is paid
questions.explanation: A choice uses resources that could have served another valuable purpose.
questions.hint: Focus on the best rejected feasible option.

questions.prompt: A free event can still have opportunity cost because:
options: Attending uses time that could have another use
Free always means costless in every sense
questions.explanation: Time is a scarce resource even without a ticket price.
questions.hint: Cost can be non-monetary.

questions.prompt: Why does scarcity require choice?
options: Every want can always be fully met
questions.explanation: Not all competing uses can be satisfied simultaneously.
questions.hint: Relate finite resources to multiple wants.

writing.prompt: Explain opportunity cost with a non-monetary example.
points: Describe the limited resource.
State the chosen activity.
Identify the next-best feasible alternative.
Explain its forgone value.

revision: Scarcity differs from having nothing.
Free of charge does not mean no opportunity cost.
The next-best alternative matters.

modules.title: Mean, median and data interpretation
modules.goal: Choose and calculate suitable measures of central tendency.

concepts.explanation: The sum of observations divided by their number.
The middle value after observations are ordered, or the mean of the two middle values for an even count.
An unusually distant observation that can strongly affect some summaries.

example.problem: Find mean and median for 2,3,3,4,18.
steps: The sum is 30, so mean=30/5=6.
The ordered middle value is 3.
The large value 18 raises the mean above most observations.
example.answer: Mean=6; median=3.

activity.prompt: Replace 18 with 180 in the example and compare the change in mean and median.
activity.check: Mean becomes 38.4; median stays 3. This illustrates sensitivity, not a rule that median is always best.

questions.prompt: Before finding a median, observations should be:
options: Converted to percentages regardless of context
questions.explanation: Position in the ordered list defines the median.
questions.hint: Middle means middle after sorting.

questions.prompt: The mean of 4,6,8 is:
questions.hint: Divide the total by the number of values.

questions.prompt: Which statement is best?
options: Mean can never be affected by an extreme value
A single average fully describes a distribution
Mean and median describe different aspects and should be chosen with context
Median always uses every numerical magnitude equally
questions.explanation: Distribution shape and purpose affect which summary is informative.
questions.hint: Consider spread and extreme observations.

writing.prompt: Explain why a report about income may include both mean and median.
points: A few large incomes can raise the mean.
Median describes the middle ordered observation.
Using both gives more context than either alone.

revision: Sort before taking the median.
Report units and sample size.
Averages do not show the whole distribution.

modules.title: Historical sources and interpretation
modules.goal: Distinguish evidence, interpretation and gaps in historical knowledge.

concepts.explanation: Evidence originating in the period or context being studied, interpreted relative to the research question.
Comparing independent evidence to test or strengthen an interpretation.
A source may omit information or reflect a particular purpose, audience and perspective.

example.problem: A royal inscription praises a ruler. How should a historian use it?
steps: Identify its date, location, audience and purpose.
Extract what it claims without assuming every claim is neutral fact.
Compare it with material remains and other records where available.
example.answer: It is evidence of royal claims and public representation, to be critically compared with other evidence.

activity.prompt: Compare a personal diary and an official announcement about the same fictional event.
activity.check: Different perspectives can reveal different information; disagreement requires investigation rather than automatic rejection.

questions.prompt: Corroboration means:
options: Assuming the oldest source is always true
questions.explanation: Comparison helps test reliability and interpretation.
questions.hint: Look for independent support.

questions.prompt: A royal praise inscription may especially reveal:
options: An entirely neutral account of every subject’s life
The exact opinion of every citizen
How a ruler wished to be represented
questions.explanation: Purpose and audience shape its representation.
questions.hint: A biased source can still be useful evidence.

questions.prompt: Why can absence of evidence fail to prove an event never happened?
options: Every claim is therefore equally valid
Records may not have survived or been discovered
questions.explanation: Survival and discovery are incomplete; claims still require evidence.
questions.hint: Distinguish an evidential gap from a disproof.

writing.prompt: Explain how a historian might evaluate an inscription.
points: Consider authorship, date, place, purpose and audience.
Distinguish claims from independent confirmation.
Compare with other relevant evidence.

revision: Ask who created a source and why.
Bias does not make a source useless.
Interpretation should remain evidence-led.

modules.title: Early cities and social organisation
modules.goal: Use material evidence to reason about urban life.

concepts.explanation: A settlement with concentrated population and specialised economic or administrative activities.
People or groups focus on particular forms of work.
An interpretation of past life based on material remains and context.

example.problem: What might standardised weights and seals suggest about an early settlement?
steps: Identify what the objects physically show.
Consider uses in exchange, accounting or identification.
Avoid assuming a complete political system from one object type alone.
example.answer: They may support organised exchange and administration, but require contextual interpretation.

activity.prompt: Design a map of a fictional early city with homes, workshops, water access and routes; explain the evidence each feature might leave.
activity.check: A map is a model, not proof about any named ancient city.

questions.prompt: Craft specialisation means:
options: Some workers focus on particular crafts
questions.explanation: Specialisation separates some tasks among groups or occupations.
questions.hint: Think about division of work.

questions.prompt: A cluster of furnaces and metal waste most directly suggests:
questions.explanation: Production debris supports an inference about craft activity.
questions.hint: Match material traces to likely activities.

questions.prompt: Why should settlement evidence be studied in context?
options: Location and associated finds affect interpretation
An object always has only one possible meaning
Context removes the need for dating
questions.explanation: Objects gain meaning from stratigraphy, surroundings and associations.
questions.hint: Ask where and alongside what the object was found.

writing.prompt: Explain how material remains can illuminate work in an early city.
points: Give two kinds of evidence.
Link each to a cautious inference.
State a limitation of the interpretation.

revision: Material evidence needs context.
Specialisation does not imply all people had equal status.
A plausible reconstruction is not a complete record.

modules.title: Constitution and limited government
modules.goal: Explain the purposes of constitutional rules and institutions.

concepts.explanation: A framework of fundamental principles and institutions for political life.
Public power is subject to rules, procedures and checks.
The principle that government authority should be constrained by constitutional norms.

example.problem: Why does an elected government still need constitutional limits?
steps: Election gives authority through a defined process.
Authority must still respect rights and legal procedures.
Checks reduce the risk of arbitrary power.
example.answer: Electoral support does not by itself authorise unlimited action.

activity.prompt: Design three rules for a classroom council that protect both majority decisions and minority participation.
activity.check: Include procedures, defined powers and an avenue to question decisions.

questions.prompt: A constitution primarily:
options: Guarantees every government decision is popular
questions.explanation: It establishes the framework within which political decisions occur.
questions.hint: Think about foundational rules.

questions.prompt: Limited government means:
options: Only a small population can vote
Government powers face legal and institutional constraints
questions.explanation: The limit concerns authority, not the absence of governance.
questions.hint: Separate constrained power from no power.

questions.prompt: Why protect minority rights in a democracy?
options: Majority decisions should not erase basic protections
questions.explanation: Democratic rule operates with constitutional protections.
questions.hint: Majority rule and rights protection must be considered together.

writing.prompt: Explain how a constitution can both enable and limit government.
points: It establishes institutions and powers.
It specifies procedures and responsibilities.
It constrains power through rights and checks.

revision: Rules can authorise as well as restrict.
Constitutionalism concerns restraint on power.
Democracy includes more than voting.

modules.title: Representation and electoral systems
modules.goal: Compare plurality voting with proportional representation conceptually.

concepts.explanation: Acting politically on behalf of others through institutions and processes.
A candidate can win a constituency by receiving more votes than any competitor, without necessarily receiving over half.
An electoral approach aiming to relate seat shares more closely to vote shares, with designs varying by system.

example.problem: Candidates receive 40%, 35% and 25% in a single-seat plurality election. Who wins?
steps: Compare the three vote shares.
The largest share is 40%.
An absolute majority is not necessary in this specified system.
example.answer: The candidate with 40% wins the seat.

activity.prompt: Compare a hypothetical party winning 40% of votes but 60% of seats; discuss why votes and seats can differ.
activity.check: Constituency distribution and electoral rules affect seat outcomes.

questions.prompt: Plurality means winning:
options: Always more than 50% of all eligible voters
More votes than any individual competitor
questions.explanation: The threshold is relative to competitors in the specified contest.
questions.hint: Largest share is not always an absolute majority.

questions.prompt: A candidate with 45% defeats candidates with 30% and 25% under:
questions.explanation: 45% is the highest share.
questions.hint: Compare the shares.

questions.prompt: Why can vote share differ from seat share?
options: Electoral rules and the geography of support matter
Every election uses identical national proportionality
Only population size determines every result
questions.explanation: The conversion depends on the institutional design and distribution of votes.
questions.hint: Distinguish counting votes from allocating seats.

writing.prompt: Compare one strength and one limitation of plurality representation.
points: Explain a straightforward constituency winner.
Discuss the link to a local representative.
Note that seat shares may differ from overall vote shares.

revision: Plurality and majority differ.
No electoral design is identical in every country.
Describe the system before evaluating results.

modules.title: Earth’s interior and plate motion
modules.goal: Connect indirect evidence with a model of Earth’s structure.

concepts.explanation: Earth’s outermost rocky layer.
A moving segment of the rigid lithosphere, which includes the crust and uppermost mantle.
Earthquake-wave behaviour helps infer the properties of Earth’s interior.

example.problem: Why does the absence of S waves through the outer core support a liquid model?
steps: S waves require shear rigidity to propagate.
Liquids do not sustain shear waves in the same way as solids.
Combine this behaviour with other seismic observations.
example.answer: S-wave behaviour is evidence that Earth’s outer core is liquid.

activity.prompt: Draw crust, mantle, outer core and inner core, then distinguish these compositional layers from the lithosphere.
activity.check: Do not equate a tectonic plate with crust alone; it includes rigid uppermost mantle.

questions.prompt: A lithospheric plate includes:
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is a mechanical layer including more than crust.
questions.hint: Distinguish crust from lithosphere.

questions.prompt: At a divergent boundary, plates generally:
questions.explanation: Divergence means separation.
questions.hint: Use the meaning of divergent.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists study seismic waves?
options: Their paths and speeds provide evidence about interior materials
They allow direct travel to the centre
They prove all mantle rock is liquid
They remove uncertainty from every Earth model
questions.explanation: Wave behaviour supports indirect inference about inaccessible regions.
questions.hint: Think about indirect observation.

writing.prompt: Explain how indirect evidence can support knowledge of Earth’s interior.
points: Identify a wave property.
Relate it to material behaviour.
Explain the inferred layer property.
Recognise that evidence is interpreted through models.

revision: The mantle is not simply a global liquid ocean.
Plates are parts of the lithosphere.
Interior knowledge uses multiple lines of evidence.

modules.title: Weather, climate and rainfall
modules.goal: Distinguish short-term conditions from long-term patterns.

concepts.explanation: Atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time.
Statistical patterns and variability of weather over long periods.
Rainfall associated with moist air rising over relief, cooling and condensing.

example.problem: Why can the windward side of a mountain receive more rain than the leeward side?
steps: Moist air is forced upward on the windward side.
Rising air expands and cools, supporting condensation if conditions permit.
Descending leeward air warms and can become relatively drier.
example.answer: Relief can create wet windward conditions and a drier rain-shadow region.

activity.prompt: Draw a mountain profile showing moist wind, ascent, clouds and descent.
activity.check: Label windward and leeward relative to the given wind direction, not a fixed compass direction.

questions.prompt: A rainy afternoon is an example of:
questions.explanation: It describes short-term atmospheric conditions.
questions.hint: Look at the time scale.

questions.prompt: The windward side is the side:
questions.explanation: Wind direction defines the term.
questions.hint: Use the incoming airflow.

questions.prompt: Why does a cold day alone not disprove a long-term warming trend?
options: Every day must be warmer than the previous day
Short-term variability and long-term trends are different
questions.explanation: A trend concerns many observations over time, not one event.
questions.hint: Distinguish an individual event from a statistical pattern.

writing.prompt: Explain orographic rainfall with a labelled sketch.
points: Show incoming moist air.
Explain ascent and cooling.
Identify windward rainfall and possible leeward rain shadow.

revision: Weather and climate differ in time scale.
Relief influences rainfall.
One event does not establish a climate trend.

modules.title: Python expressions, types and decisions
modules.goal: Trace simple Python expressions and conditional logic.

concepts.explanation: A name bound to an object or value in Python.
The category of a value, such as int, float, str or bool.
An if statement executes a block when its condition evaluates as true.

example.problem: Trace: x=7; if x%2==0: result="even"; else: result="odd".
steps: 7%2 gives remainder 1.
1==0 is False.
The else branch assigns "odd".
example.answer: result is "odd".

activity.prompt: Write pseudocode that classifies a positive integer as even or odd, then try 2, 7 and 10.
activity.check: Check remainder after division by 2; zero means even.

questions.prompt: In Python, 7//2 evaluates to:
questions.explanation: For these positive integers, // gives the floor quotient.
questions.hint: Distinguish / from //.

questions.prompt: Which value has type str?
questions.explanation: Quotes make this a string rather than a numeric literal.
questions.hint: Look for quotation marks.

questions.prompt: For x=5, which condition is true?
questions.explanation: Both comparisons in the first expression are true.
questions.hint: Evaluate each comparison before the logical operator.

writing.prompt: Explain how a program chooses between two branches.
points: Evaluate the condition.
Execute the if block when true.
Execute the else block when false, if present.
Indent blocks correctly.

revision: = assigns; == compares.
Types affect valid operations.
Trace values one step at a time.

modules.title: Loops, lists and trace tables
modules.goal: Use iteration to process a small sequence.

concepts.explanation: An ordered mutable sequence in Python.
Repeated execution over items or while a condition holds.
A variable updated to build a result such as a sum.

example.problem: Trace total=0; for n in [2,4,6]: total=total+n.
steps: Start total at 0.
After n=2, total=2.
After n=4, total=6.
After n=6, total=12.
example.answer: Final total is 12.

activity.prompt: Create a trace table for counting values greater than 5 in [3,8,5,9].
activity.check: The count is 2; 5 itself does not satisfy greater than 5.

questions.prompt: Python list indexing starts at:
questions.explanation: The first item has index 0.
questions.hint: Distinguish position number from Python index.

questions.explanation: Length counts items, including repeated values.
questions.hint: Count entries, not distinct values.

questions.prompt: What is the sum after processing [1,2,3] from total=0 with total+=n?
questions.explanation: The accumulator becomes 1, then 3, then 6.
questions.hint: Trace each iteration.

writing.prompt: Explain an accumulator loop using a trace table.
points: Show the initial value.
Record the current item each iteration.
Record the updated accumulator.
State the final result.

revision: Repeated values are separate list items.
Initialisation affects the result.
A trace table helps reveal logic errors.

modules.title: Psychological research and evidence
modules.goal: Distinguish variables, correlation and controlled investigation.

concepts.explanation: A characteristic that can vary across people or conditions.
An association between variables; by itself it does not establish causation.
A factor that may offer an alternative explanation for an observed relationship.

example.problem: Students who sleep longer also score higher in a survey. Does the survey prove sleep caused the difference?
steps: Identify the association.
Consider other factors such as health, workload or study conditions.
A survey alone does not isolate the causal contribution.
example.answer: The result is an association; further evidence is needed for a causal claim.

activity.prompt: Design an anonymous, voluntary survey about study habits without collecting names or sensitive health details.
activity.check: Use consent and clear questions; do not diagnose people from survey responses.

questions.prompt: Correlation alone establishes:
options: A proven cause in every case
questions.explanation: A relationship can reflect reverse influence or another factor.
questions.hint: Ask whether alternative explanations were controlled.

questions.prompt: A confound is:
options: A factor offering an alternative explanation
questions.explanation: Confounds can distort an apparent causal interpretation.
questions.hint: Look for another variable connected to the outcome.

questions.prompt: Why should participation be voluntary?
options: Research should respect informed choice and welfare
It guarantees the hypothesis is true
questions.explanation: Ethical research respects autonomy and minimises harm.
questions.hint: Ethical duties are distinct from statistical results.

writing.prompt: Explain why a survey finding should be interpreted cautiously.
points: Identify sampling and measurement limits.
Distinguish association from causation.
Mention possible alternative explanations.
Respect privacy and consent.

revision: Do not infer causation from association alone.
Operational definitions matter.
Psychological research requires ethical safeguards.

modules.title: Learning, encoding and retrieval
modules.goal: Apply retrieval practice without confusing familiarity with recall.

concepts.explanation: Processes by which information is initially represented in memory.
Accessing information from memory.
Distributing study across separated sessions rather than one uninterrupted block.

example.problem: A student recognises every highlighted sentence but cannot explain the topic with the book closed. What should change?
steps: Recognition can feel easier than unaided retrieval.
Close the book and answer a focused question.
Check the response and revisit gaps after a delay.
example.answer: Combine retrieval attempts, corrective feedback and spaced review.

activity.prompt: Study five terms, close the notes, write their meanings, then check and repeat the missed ones tomorrow.
activity.check: Judge learning using what can be retrieved and explained, not only how familiar the page feels.

questions.prompt: Retrieval practice involves:
options: Trying to recall information before checking
questions.explanation: The learner attempts to bring information to mind.
questions.hint: The key action occurs with the answer hidden.

questions.prompt: Spacing means:
options: Doing all study without breaks once
questions.explanation: Distributed sessions separate learning opportunities in time.
questions.hint: Think about when sessions occur.

questions.prompt: Why check answers after recall?
options: Feedback can correct errors and guide later study
questions.explanation: Feedback helps avoid retaining an incorrect response.
questions.hint: Retrieval and correction serve complementary roles.

writing.prompt: Design a one-week study routine using retrieval and spacing.
points: Include initial study.
Schedule brief closed-book recall sessions.
Check errors and revisit them later.
Use explanations as well as recognition questions.

revision: Familiarity is not identical to recall.
Feedback matters after mistakes.
Practice benefits depend on the task and conditions.

modules.title: Sociological imagination and social context
modules.goal: Connect personal experiences with wider social arrangements.

concepts.explanation: Examining how social relationships, institutions and structures shape experience.
An established pattern of social organisation, such as education or family.
The historical and social conditions surrounding an action or experience.

example.problem: Why might different students have different study time after school?
steps: Personal choices matter, but examine commuting, paid work and care responsibilities.
Consider access to space, devices and support.
Avoid assuming one explanation fits every student.
example.answer: Study routines are shaped by both agency and social conditions.

activity.prompt: Use a fictional student to map one personal choice and three social conditions affecting study.
activity.check: Explain a relationship without stereotyping a whole community.

questions.prompt: A sociological question is:
options: Can all differences be blamed on laziness?
What is one person’s favourite colour with no further context?
How do transport and household responsibilities affect study time?
questions.explanation: It links an experience to social conditions and patterns.
questions.hint: Look beyond an isolated judgement.

questions.prompt: Education is an example of a:
questions.explanation: It is an organised and enduring pattern of social activity.
questions.hint: Think about structured social arrangements.

questions.prompt: Why use several cases rather than one anecdote to describe a pattern?
options: A large claim is always true
One case may not represent wider variation
questions.explanation: Broader claims require evidence suited to their scope.
questions.hint: Match the evidence to the scale of the claim.

writing.prompt: Explain a daily experience using personal choice and social context.
points: Describe the experience.
Identify relevant institutions or conditions.
Explain a plausible connection.
Avoid treating the example as proof about everyone.

revision: Agency and structure can interact.
Context is not an excuse to ignore evidence.
Avoid stereotypes and unsupported generalisations.

modules.title: Socialisation, norms and roles
modules.goal: Explain how social expectations are learned and negotiated.

concepts.explanation: The continuing process through which people learn social practices, meanings and expectations.
A socially shared expectation about behaviour in a context.
Expectations associated with a social position or relationship.

example.problem: A student behaves differently in a classroom and on a sports field. Explain without assuming insincerity.
steps: Different contexts involve different norms and roles.
Classroom participation and team competition may call for different behaviour.
People interpret and negotiate expectations rather than simply copy them.
example.answer: Behaviour can vary because contexts and role expectations differ.

activity.prompt: List two expectations of a class representative and two of a team captain; identify one possible conflict.
activity.check: Roles can overlap, and expectations can change across groups and time.

questions.prompt: Socialisation occurs:
options: Only on the day of birth
questions.explanation: New settings and relationships continue to shape learning.
questions.hint: Think about learning new roles as an adult.

questions.prompt: A norm is:
questions.explanation: Sociological norms concern expected conduct, often unwritten.
questions.hint: Separate social expectation from legal rule.

questions.prompt: Role conflict can occur when:
options: Expectations from different roles are incompatible
A person has no social relationships
questions.explanation: Competing demands can make satisfying both roles difficult.
questions.hint: Consider two obligations scheduled at the same time.

writing.prompt: Explain norms and roles using a school example.
points: Identify a context.
State an expectation in that context.
Identify the associated role.
Discuss possible variation or conflict.

revision: Norms may be unwritten.
Roles are learned and interpreted.
Social expectations can change.
